newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore focuses on economic growth, Malaysia row.
newsitem.headline: Singapore focuses on economic growth, Malaysia row.

text.p: Singapore's new parliament began its first working session on Monday with members addressing how the city-state can maintain its economic growth and expressing concern over a spat with Malaysia.

The dispute began when Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew said in a court affidavit made public earlier this year that Malaysia's Johor Baru was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings", sparking a heated response from Malaysia.
Lee twice apologised for the remarks, which aroused harsh criticism from Malaysia, much of it directed against Lee personally.

Some members of parliament, in their first policy debate since January elections won by the People's Action Party, which has ruled Singapore since 1959, expressed disappointment the row had dragged on for months, despite the apologies.
One MP quoted a constituent as saying: "As a Malay and a Moslem I'm ashamed of the extremist attitude displayed by some of the people across the causeway."
A short causeway separates Singapore from Malaysia.

The dispute has spilled over into other areas, including tourism, investment and shipping. The two countries "are going through difficult bilateral relations", Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar said on Saturday.
Several MPs said the row was detrimental to the stability of the region and would hinder economic growth of both countries.
With Singapore's neighbours boosting their own port, airport and financial services, some MPs said relations with Malaysia were among factors requiring a change of mindset in Singapore.
They said Singaporeans were vulnerable because of scarce resources and a small domestic market and could not afford complacency.
"It is productivity growth that ultimately determines real income and economic growth," said MP Loh Meng See. He said productivity had slowed recently.
"If not sustained, it will affect competitiveness, hurt our exports and growth prospects," Loh said, noting that many older workers had skills that would soon become obsolete.
Others said such structural unemployment in the near future would create social displacement.
